catalog_quote: The phonological word is a stress group within which syllables are distributed and it is itself distributed within the phonological phrase. It is composed of an obligatory nucleus with optional preceeding and/or following margins. Primary stress (') occurs once in each phonological word, predictably on the penultimate syllable of each morpheme occupying the nuclear position. Reduplicated words behave as two separate words in this respect. Primary stress is phonetically defined by slightly higher pitch, intensity and length. new_statements.quote: The phonological word is a stress group within which syllables are distributed and it is itself distributed within the phonological phrase. It is composed of an obligatory nucleus with optional preceeding and/or following margins. Primary stress ( ' ) occurs once in each phonological word, predictably on the penultimate syllable of each morpheme occupying the nuclear position. Reduplicated words behave as two separate words in this respect. Primary stress is phonetically defined by slightly higher pitch, intensity and length. [p. 163, sec. 7.1:] Stress occurs on the nucleus of each phonological word with the effect of rising pitch, intensity and adding slightly to the length of the vowel.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word, falling predictably on the penultimate syllable of the root (nuclear) morpheme; margin morphemes (minor morphemes) are unstressed; each half of a reduplicated word carries its own penultimate stress. Stress is cued by slightly higher pitch, intensity and length; vowel length is not contrastive and apparent long vowels are intensified stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; only primary stress described ('occurs once in each phonological word'). Phrase-level intonation (sec. 5) rides on the stressed syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Reduplicated words behave as two separate words for stress ([polj'polji] 'morning' after vowel loss, sec. 6.2). Sec. 7.1 (pp. 163-164): earlier reports of vowel length by Durrad (1910) and Firth (1963) are reinterpreted; ['ma:tea] 'much' has normal stress in normal speech but in isolation/excitement 'could be said to have length on the first syllable. I prefer to regard this as stress which may be intensified in exclamations'; isolated vowel words in reply may be lengthened predictably.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (= stress group) inside the phonological phrase: an obligatory nucleus (root morpheme) with optional preceding/following margins (minor morphemes/clitics), so stress sits on the penult of the root, not of the whole clitic group; reduplicated words are two stress domains; any syllable type can be a monosyllabic word (stressed, e.g. /ka/ ['ka]). Based on 1974 fieldwork; connected-speech examples and phrase intonation (sec. 5) also given.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Tikopia proper (tiko1237, ISO tkp); Dodenhoff's data come from 1974 fieldwork with Tikopia speakers at Nukufero (Russell Is.), Nukukaisi (San Cristobal/Makira), Honiara and Namo on Tikopia island; he states there is 'little or no difference in dialects' between the home island and the colonies. No separate variety involved.
